q: Does adding a noise-aware reward term (e.g. minimize expected error under a realistic depolarizing / T1-T2 noise model) change which schedule the PPO agent converges to, and does it beat noise-oblivious ALAP on fidelity rather than cycle count?
basis: The paper's Scheduling PoC optimizes cycle count only, with reward -5/-1/0. Real quantum compilation trades depth for fidelity: a shorter noisy schedule can be worse than a slightly longer schedule that avoids error-prone gates or crosstalk windows. qgym's Rewarder is pluggable but the paper does not exercise noise-awareness. This is the single most important extension for the framework to matter to hardware groups.
next_steps: Subclass qgym BasicRewarder to add a per-gate fidelity penalty computed from a Qiskit NoiseModel (T1/T2 + depolarizing per gate type). Retrain PPO 1e5 steps at seed 20260703 on 3-qubit MachineProperties. Evaluate both PPO and ALAP under simulation with the same noise model; report mean process fidelity and mean cycle count. Success criterion: PPO strictly beats ALAP on fidelity even if it ties or loses on cycle count.

q: Do modern off-policy or model-based RL algorithms (SAC, DreamerV3, MuZero-style) reach ALAP-parity in materially fewer environment steps than vanilla PPO on the qgym Scheduling PoC, and do they scale to larger circuits where PPO stalls?
basis: The paper's PoC uses only vanilla PPO and only reports the 1e5-step curve. Our replication showed PPO's convergence is hyperparameter-sensitive (n_steps=256 collapses; n_steps=2048 works). Off-policy methods with replay buffers and world models are typically far more sample-efficient on discrete-action combinatorial tasks and would be the natural next algorithmic axis to test.
next_steps: Wrap qgym Scheduling in a Gymnasium-compatible adapter compatible with cleanrl or SB3-contrib. Train SAC-Discrete and a small DreamerV3 on the same 3-qubit / max_gates=5 setup with matched seed. Compare (i) sample steps to first reach ALAP-mean-cycles parity, and (ii) final mean cycles on a held-out 50-circuit test set drawn with seeds 20261703..20261752. Report per-algorithm sample efficiency curves.

q: How does a qgym-trained Scheduling agent perform on real hardware topologies (IBM Heron/Eagle, IonQ linear, Rigetti Aspen) as opposed to the synthetic 3-qubit MachineProperties the paper uses, and does the trained policy transfer or does it need retraining per topology?
basis: The paper's PoC uses an abstract 3-qubit machine with no coupling constraints. Real compilation targets have specific coupling maps, native gate sets, and asymmetric gate durations. Whether the qgym RL approach generalizes to production hardware is entirely untested by the paper.
next_steps: Instantiate three qgym MachineProperties matching (i) IBM Eagle 27q heavy-hex sub-lattice, (ii) IonQ 11q all-to-all linear, (iii) Rigetti Aspen-M lattice fragment. Train PPO per-topology on random 10-gate circuits. Then evaluate each trained agent on the other two topologies and report the transfer gap (mean cycles delta vs a topology-specific ALAP baseline). Success = zero-shot transfer within 10% of ALAP on unseen topologies.

q: Can a policy pre-trained on one hardware topology be fine-tuned to a new topology in far fewer steps than training from scratch, and if so what representation (graph-neural-network state encoder vs the qgym default MLP) gives the best transfer?
basis: Transfer learning across coupling maps is the practically useful version of the previous question. qgym's default MultiInputPolicy uses a flat MLP over dict observations; GNNs over the coupling graph are the standard architectural choice in the graph-RL literature (e.g. Fawzi et al. AlphaTensor-style) and are the obvious ablation.
next_steps: Implement a GNN feature extractor for qgym Scheduling observations (nodes = qubits, edges = coupling). Pre-train PPO on topology A for 1e5 steps, then continue training on topology B for 1e4, 5e3, 2.5e3 steps. Compare to training from scratch on B under the same budgets. Metric: cycles-to-ALAP-parity vs cumulative environment steps. Baseline = flat MLP under the same protocol.

q: In a hybrid ML-in-the-loop setup, can a qgym-trained agent be inserted as a heuristic inside Qiskit or t|ket>'s transpiler pass manager to strictly improve on the classical compiler's schedule depth on realistic (20-50 qubit) benchmark circuits, or does the classical compiler dominate at that scale?
basis: The most useful home for a qgym-trained agent is not to replace a classical compiler but to be a callable subroutine inside one (e.g. a scheduling pass sitting between routing and gate synthesis in Qiskit's PassManager). The paper does not test integration with a real compiler. Whether the RL agent is even a net positive when combined with mature classical passes is unknown.
next_steps: Write a Qiskit TransformationPass that calls a trained qgym Scheduling agent to schedule each basic block, keeping Qiskit's routing and synthesis passes unchanged. Run the hybrid vs stock Qiskit transpile at optimization_level=3 on QASMBench medium (20 qubits) and QASMBench large (40-50 qubits). Compare (i) circuit depth, (ii) two-qubit gate count, (iii) transpile wall time. Success = hybrid strictly beats stock Qiskit on depth without regressing gate count.
